about.title: Hillsborough Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Hillsborough is a quiet residential community in San Mateo County, but its households still rely on landscapers, contractors, domestic staff, delivery crews, and tradespeople who move through the area's estates and job sites every day. When one of these workers gets hurt, California law generally routes the claim through workers' compensation, regardless of who was at fault, and that process leaves no room to sue the employer directly in most cases. But that's not the whole picture. If a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver on a road like I-280 or Skyline Boulevard contributed to the injury, a separate claim against that third party may be possible, and it wouldn't be limited by the workers' comp system. We handle workplace injury claims and can help sort out which paths apply and explain them in plain terms.

items.title: We Help Sort Comp From Third-Party Claims
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against an employer, but a negligent third party like a subcontractor or equipment maker can open a separate claim. We can help figure out which applies to your situation.

items.title: We Know the Reporting Clock Matters
items.desc: California generally requires injuries be reported to an employer within 30 days, and missing that window can complicate a claim. We work quickly so you're not navigating deadlines alone.

items.title: We Understand Retaliation Concerns Are Real
items.desc: It's illegal for an employer to retaliate against someone for reporting a workplace injury. If you're worried about your job, we can talk through your rights before you decide anything.

items.question: I was hurt while doing landscaping work at a Hillsborough property. Can I file more than one type of claim?
items.answer: It's possible. Workers' compensation typically covers the employer relationship regardless of fault, but if a property owner, equipment supplier, or another driver contributed to the injury, a separate third-party claim may be available. We can review the details of your specific situation.

items.question: How long do I have to report my injury to my employer?
items.answer: California generally expects an injury to be reported within 30 days of when it happened. Waiting longer can make the claim harder to support, so it's worth acting promptly even if the injury seemed minor at first.

items.question: What if my injury happened while driving on I-280 or Skyline Boulevard for work?
items.answer: If another driver caused the crash, that could support a third-party injury claim separate from workers' comp, and those claims generally carry a two-year deadline in California. We can help you understand how the timing and facts of your case fit together.
